strengths: The core idea—using average pairwise cosine distance as a simple, label-free geometric statistic—is intuitive, easy to compute, and the paper is clearly written with a well-organized empirical narrative.

The paper attempts to go beyond a purely descriptive observation by proposing several downstream applications (accuracy estimation, model selection, layer selection, and a training objective), which is the right instinct for making anisotropy/dispersion findings actionable.

Broad empirical coverage for the main correlation: many model families (Llama, Qwen, Gemma, Mistral, Phi), multiple domains (WikiText, CNN/DailyMail, PubMed), and layer-wise/fine-tuning analyses, with full visualizations and reasonably documented hyperparameters in the appendix.

The semantic-cluster analysis (§3.3), showing that within-cluster dispersion also grows during training, is a nice control that partially rules out the trivial 'only dissimilar contexts separate' explanation.
weaknesses: Unsupported central claim in §4.3: the abstract and intro claim dispersion can 'pinpoint the best representations for retrieval-based methods such as kNN-LM, bypassing exhaustive layer-by-layer searches,' but the paper never actually runs kNN-LM or reports any kNN-LM perplexity. It only shows that attention sub-layer embeddings are more dispersed than FFN embeddings and cites Xu et al. (2023) for the claim that attention output works better. The leap from 'more dispersed' to 'better retrieval key' is asserted, not demonstrated.

The headline correlation is potentially confounded and the causal story is not established. Perplexity and dispersion are measured on the same text, so semantically similar segments are simultaneously more similar in embedding space (lower dispersion) and likely share perplexity levels; token frequency/domain closeness could drive both. The paper acknowledges no causality in the Limitations, but the abstract's framing ('ability to predict text is tightly linked to breadth') overstates what a correlation across perplexity bins supports.

§4.1 is a largely tautological experiment: accuracy levels are synthetically constructed by sampling different mixtures of correct and incorrect queries, so the input distribution changes with the 'accuracy' level by construction. Ground-truth labels are used to build the experiment, contradicting the 'without labeled data' framing, and no experiment actually predicts a model's real accuracy on an unseen dataset from dispersion alone.

§4.2 (model selection) is small-scale and weakly controlled: only 9 Qwen checkpoints and 4 Llama/CodeLlama checkpoints, with model size and fine-tuning confounded (e.g., Distill-Qwen variants dominate both gap and accuracy, making perfect ranking nearly trivial). The 'dispersion gap' is computed on static output token-embedding rows, which is a different quantity from the contextual dispersion the core claim is about, weakening the conceptual link.

§4.4 training experiments are toy-scale (GPT-2 small, 500–1000 steps, perplexities of 80–300), with small gains in the single-domain setting (1–4 points) and no comparison against alternative regularization baselines or significance testing; the cross-domain gains could reflect the cross-domain loss acting as domain separation rather than 'dispersion' per se.

Limited novelty relative to prior work: the anisotropy/narrow-cone literature (Mu & Viswanath 2018, Ethayarajh 2019, Gao et al. 2019, Li et al. 2020) already established that LLM embedding geometry correlates with model quality; the closest work (Viswanathan et al. 2025) is characterized as 'descriptive,' but the delta here is mainly repackaging the same correlation into applications whose evaluations are themselves weak.

Presentation concerns: Figure 2 is labeled 'An Illustrative Empirical Trend' and appears to be a synthetic illustration rather than real data, which is inappropriate for the paper's headline empirical claim; the code-availability footnote is truncated/empty; some reported correlations are much weaker than claimed (e.g., r = -0.25 for Medical/Llama-3.1-8B), which the text glosses over.

strengths: The paper covers a broad empirical sweep: multiple model families (Llama, Gemma, Qwen, Mistral, Phi, GPT-2), multiple domains (WikiText, CNN/DailyMail, PubMed), and layer-wise analyses, with extensive appendix visualizations.

The core observation—that final-layer contextual embeddings of lower-perplexity text are more dispersed—is clearly stated and easy to reproduce, and the semantic-cluster analysis (§3.3) is a nice attempt to rule out a trivial 'dissimilar contexts spread apart' explanation.
Writing and organization are generally clear, and the paper is honest in its Limitations section that causality cannot be concluded.
weaknesses: Overstated central claim relative to evidence. The abstract asserts dispersion 'strongly and negatively correlates' with perplexity, but the headline Figure 2 is explicitly labeled an 'Illustrative Empirical Trend' (apparently synthetic), and the actual correlations include substantially weaker cases (e.g., Medical/Llama-3.1-8B r=-0.25, WikiText/Gemma-2-2B r=-0.47). Presenting a cartoon/illustrative figure as the empirical anchor of the paper is misleading.

The core correlation is confounded and largely re-describes known anisotropy findings. Gao et al. (2019), Ethayarajh (2019), etc. already established that better-trained LMs spread representations into a wider cone; the paper mostly re-observes this at the sequence level without isolating confounds (sequence length, repetition/templating of high-perplexity text, token frequency) that could trivially drive the correlation.

§4.1 (label-free accuracy prediction) is close to tautological. The experiment constructs mixtures of known-correct and known-incorrect queries and shows mean pairwise distance tracks the mixture fraction. This merely confirms that correct samples have higher average dispersion than incorrect ones—it does not establish dispersion as a usable accuracy estimator. Critically, there is no comparison to obvious label-free baselines such as per-sample model confidence/entropy (which requires no labels either), and no per-sample ROC/calibration analysis.

§4.3 (layer selection for kNN-LM) never runs kNN-LM. The experiments only show that attention-sub-layer outputs are more dispersed than FFN outputs, and then cite Xu et al. (2023) that attention outputs happen to improve kNN-LM. The claim that dispersion 'pinpoints the best representations for retrieval-based methods' is therefore unsupported by any end-to-end kNN-LM perplexity evaluation.

§4.2 (model selection) rests on only ~9 checkpoints with strong prior confounds (Distill-Qwen and CodeLlama are known-better variants), and a 'perfect ranking of nine checkpoints' with Spearman > 0.95 on n=9 is weak statistical evidence. The 'dispersion gap' is computed on static token embeddings, a different quantity from the contextual dispersion analyzed in §3, weakening the narrative coherence.

Table 3 reports 'Cosine Distances' exceeding 1 (e.g., D–NM = 1.11, 1.16), which is impossible for properly normalized cosine distance of token embedding rows as described, suggesting an inconsistent metric or reporting error that undermines confidence in the model-selection results.

§4.4 (push-away loss) is very small scale and undercontrolled: GPT-2 small trained for only 500–1000 steps to perplexities of ~80–300, improvements of 1–4 points in the single-domain case, and no comparison against standard regularizers (weight decay, dropout) or existing contrastive objectives (SupCon, ContraCLM), to which it is essentially adjacent. The cross-domain gains are plausibly just domain-separation effects rather than evidence for the dispersion–quality hypothesis.

Missing baselines and ablations throughout: no comparison of dispersion against intrinsic dimension, entropy, or embedding-norm statistics; the layer-selection and fine-tuning sections would need correlations across more architectures to be convincing.

Reproducibility is incomplete: footnote 1 says 'Code is available at' with an empty link, and several key details (bin sizes for Figure 3, how uniform perplexity sampling affects the correlation estimates) are under-specified.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and well-organized, with an intuitive central hypothesis connecting embedding dispersion to predictive quality.

The empirical trend (dispersion vs. perplexity) is evaluated across a reasonably broad set of model families (Llama, Gemma, Mistral, Phi, Qwen) and three text domains, with consistent negative correlations documented in extensive appendix visualizations.

The fine-grained analysis in §3.3 (within-cluster vs. between-cluster dispersion over semantically similar contexts sharing 10-gram continuations) is a thoughtful control that goes beyond naive global averages.
The proposed dispersion-gap metric for model selection is extremely cheap (embedding-matrix-only, CPU, no forward passes), which is attractive if validated.
Hyperparameters and training details are documented in the appendices, and a limitations section is provided.
weaknesses: A major confound is never addressed: dispersion is computed across sets of text segments, so it depends on the content similarity of the inputs themselves. Bins sorted by perplexity may differ systematically in textual redundancy/semantic diversity, meaning low dispersion could reflect input homogeneity rather than model quality. Only §3.3 partially mitigates this, and only for the training-dynamics analysis.

§4.1's headline claim ('predict downstream accuracy without labeled data') is validated with a synthetic, partially circular protocol: accuracy levels are constructed by mixing known-correct and known-incorrect predictions. This demonstrates that correct items are individually more dispersed, but does not establish that dispersion estimates the accuracy of a naturally distributed unlabeled query set.

§4.3 (kNN-LM layer selection) never actually runs kNN-LM. The paper only shows the attention sub-layer is more dispersive than the FFN sub-layer and cites Xu et al. (2023) for the performance claim; the proposed application ('bypassing exhaustive layer-by-layer searches') is asserted, not demonstrated. Also, Table 1 shows the gap between sub-layers is enormous (e.g., 0.66 vs. 0.19), so the result is likely trivial and would be obvious from any cheap end-to-end trial.

§4.2 evaluates the dispersion gap on only 9 checkpoints (Qwen/MATH) and 4 checkpoints (Llama/CodeLlama) with trivially known orderings (base vs. math-tuned vs. distilled; Llama2 vs. CodeLlama). A Spearman correlation above 0.95 on n=9 with perfectly distinguishable checkpoints is weak evidence, and no comparison is made against the obvious label-free baseline: simply computing perplexity (or likelihood/MDL) on unlabeled target-domain text.

§4.4's training experiments are very limited: GPT-2 small trained for only 500–1000 steps (final perplexities of 82–226 indicate severe undertraining), improvements of 1–4 perplexity points in the single-domain setting, no error bars or multiple seeds, and the 'push-away' idea substantially overlaps existing contrastive/uniformity objectives (e.g., ContraCLM, cited but not compared against).

Figure 2 in the introduction is explicitly labeled 'An Illustrative Empirical Trend' but appears to be schematic/synthetic; presenting an illustrative plot in place of real data in the intro is misleading.

Several observed correlations are quite weak for specific model/domain pairs (e.g., r = -0.25 for Llama-3.1-8B on PubMed, p = 0.017), and the strength of the effect varies substantially across models, which is not analyzed or explained.

No theoretical grounding for why dispersion should cause (rather than merely accompany) better prediction; the causal direction is acknowledged as unresolved in the limitations, yet the abstract and applications sections repeatedly use causal language ('identifying layers... pinpoints the best representations').

The scope of the methodological contribution is narrow: the core metric is average pairwise cosine distance, and each application is a small, individually under-powered experiment rather than a convincing demonstration of a reusable tool.

strengths: The paper is well-executed empirically across many model families (Llama, Qwen, Gemma, Mistral, Phi) and domains (WikiText, news, PubMed), with consistent negative correlations between dispersion and perplexity (r between -0.25 and -0.93), and a metric-robustness check using the Vendi Score that rules out an artifact of the cosine-distance metric.

The controlled hardness-slicing experiment is clever: dispersion is strongly monotone in the fraction of correct answers while perplexity is nearly flat (Tables 3-4), suggesting dispersion carries signal beyond next-token confidence; the calibration experiment (MAE 1.4-2.2 points on held-out MMLU) adds concrete quantitative support for practical utility.

The model-selection analysis is strengthened by a high-resolution check over 30 Olmo-7B training checkpoints (Spearman ~0.90-0.95) rather than only static model comparisons, and the 'squeeze' ablation (Table 13) provides evidence in the direction of causality rather than mere correlation.

The dispersion metric is extremely cheap to compute (CPU-only for the model-selection variant, ~5,000 tokens for kNN-LM layer profiling), which makes the proposed applications genuinely practical, and the paper is transparent about limitations and LLM usage.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to prior work: the core observation is closely aligned with the anisotropy / intrinsic-dimension / embedding-geometry literature (Ethayarajh 2019, Valeriani et al. 2023, Viswanathan et al. 2025) and with the Vendi score; the paper's own related-work section concedes the closest study is largely descriptive, but the delta here is mostly packaging known observations into applications rather than a new insight or theory.

The kNN-LM application (Section 3.3) is claimed but never validated end-to-end: the paper never actually runs kNN-LM and reports perplexity for the dispersion-selected layer versus alternatives; the entire argument rests on the prior observation (Xu et al., 2023) that attention outputs help kNN-LM plus the fact that attention outputs happen to be more dispersed. This leaves a central application claim unsupported.

The hardness-ranking protocol is somewhat artificial: slices are constructed by mixing known-correct and known-incorrect examples at controlled fractions, then measuring mean dispersion of the mixture. This does not directly demonstrate per-example difficulty ranking or slice discovery on naturally occurring unlabeled data, which is the claimed use case.

Model-selection experiments are narrow: only 9 Qwen variants on MATH and 4 Llama/CodeLlama checkpoints on HumanEval, restricted to the same model family and tokenizer, with hand-picked domain token sets; the metric explicitly fails across families, limiting general utility, and there is a risk of circularity (Distill-Qwen models are independently known to be much stronger).

Training experiments are very small-scale: GPT-2 small trained for only 500-1000 steps on WikiText, at perplexities (83-226) far from convergence; perplexity gains of 1-4 points (single-domain) could disappear or reverse with longer training, and the cross-domain result is presented without a compute-matched baseline discussion or more than one model.

Possible confounders are not fully addressed: dispersion depends on segment content, length, and domain mixture; Figure 1 is purely illustrative; and several correlation results weaken substantially in some settings (e.g., r = -0.25 for PubMed on Llama-3.1-8B), which the main text does not discuss.
Writing quality issues (e.g., 'di scriminative', 'e ffects', double punctuation, incomplete footnote for the code link) suggest insufficient polish for a camera-ready submission.

strengths: Broad empirical scope: the core perplexity–dispersion correlation is examined across many model families (Llama, Gemma, Mistral, Phi, Qwen), scales, and domains (WikiText, CNN/DailyMail, PubMed), with extensive appendix visualizations.
The central metric (average pairwise cosine distance) is simple, cheap to compute, and the paper is transparent about its computational cost (a few thousand tokens suffice for stable estimates).
The 'squeeze' ablation (Appendix B.4.2) is a nice touch that goes beyond pure correlational evidence by penalizing dispersion and observing performance degradation.
Comparison against perplexity as a competing label-free hardness signal (B.1.2) is a sensible attempt to show dispersion is not merely a proxy for next-token confidence.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the link between embedding anisotropy/isotropy and model quality is well established (Ethayarajh 2019; Gao et al. 2019; uniformity/diversity metrics such as the Vendi score; intrinsic-dimension analyses). The paper largely re-confirms known intuition with a simpler statistic, and the closest related work (Viswanathan et al., 2025) is acknowledged but the differentiation ('they are descriptive, we are actionable') is thin.

The kNN-LM application (§3.3) is never actually evaluated: the paper only measures dispersion of sub-layer outputs and asserts that the attention output is the 'natural choice' of key. No kNN-LM perplexity numbers are reported for any layer, so the claimed unsupervised shortcut is unvalidated end-to-end. This is a serious gap for one of the four headline contributions.

Model selection results (§3.2) rest on tiny samples (9 Qwen checkpoints, 4 Llama/CodeLlama pairs), where Spearman >0.95 is unsurprising. Worse, the reported numbers contain an internal inconsistency: under cosine distance (Table 12), Llama2's dispersion gap exceeds CodeLlama's (1.9255 vs 1.9087) despite CodeLlama's much higher HumanEval, suggesting the metric is cherry-picked (Euclidean) to fit the narrative. Correlations with accuracy may also just track parameter scale / fine-tuning, a confound not controlled.

The label-free hardness analysis (§3.1) is confounded: as the fraction of correct answers varies, the composition of the sampled query pool changes, so dispersion differences may reflect differences in question content/lexical diversity rather than model hardness. A matched-question design is needed; the protocol also requires ground-truth labels for its construction, undermining the 'label-free' framing in the abstract.

Training experiments (§3.4) are weak: only GPT-2-SMALL, only 500–1000 training steps (test perplexities of 80–300, far from a trained regime), single-domain gains of only 1–4 points, and no comparison against any existing regularizer (InfoNCE, uniformity losses, whitening/anisotropy corrections) despite the appendix admitting the push-away loss is a simplified contrastive objective. The 'squeeze' baseline (collapsing embeddings to a point) is a degenerate strawman.

Correlational analyses on binned data report Pearson r with 'p = 0.000' as if bins were independent samples; the statistical treatment is inappropriate and the effect sizes are modest in several settings (e.g., r = -0.25 for Llama-3.1-8B on PubMed, with the trend visibly noisier for 8B models than smaller ones — the opposite of what a 'stronger models disperse more' story would suggest).

Cross-model comparisons in §2 conflate within-model sample hardness with between-model quality: larger models both have lower perplexity and (plausibly) larger dispersion, so the headline 'higher dispersion predicts lower perplexity across model families' risks being a scale artifact rather than a geometric insight.
Missing URL in the code footnote ('Code is available at' — empty), harming reproducibility claims; Figure 2 is explicitly 'illustrative' rather than actual data, and Figures 1–2 are schematic.

Scope of applications is narrower than claimed: the model-selection metric requires hand-picked domain token sets (digits, Python keywords, legal terms) and is only validated within a fixed family and tokenizer, limiting practical utility.

strengths: The paper connects embedding geometry (average pairwise cosine dispersion) to LM performance and demonstrates the relationship across a genuinely broad set of model families (Llama, Gemma, Mistral, Phi, Qwen) and domains (WikiText, news, PubMed, and QA benchmarks), with per-model correlation statistics reported in extensive appendices.

The paper goes beyond correlation: it includes both a 'push-away' auxiliary loss that increases dispersion and lowers perplexity, and a converse 'squeeze' ablation that penalizes dispersion and degrades perplexity, which together provide stronger (though still small-scale) evidence for a functional link rather than a mere artifact.

Several proposed applications are practical and label-free (hard-slice discovery, calibration of accuracy from dispersion with ~1.4–2.2 pp MAE, a CPU-only 'dispersion gap' model-selection score), and the comparison against perplexity as a competing hardness signal (Appendix B.1.2) shows dispersion is not reducible to token confidence.

Metric robustness is checked with the Vendi Score, held-out test splits, distribution-shift datasets (HellaSwag_chat, IFEval, QuAIL), and a 30-checkpoint Olmo-7B training-trajectory analysis with high Spearman correlations.
Reproducibility is supported by detailed hyperparameters, sampling procedures (Algorithm 1), and a stated code release; limitations are candidly discussed.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core observation is a natural extension of the well-known anisotropy / representation-collapse literature (Ethayarajh 2019, Gao et al. 2019, Valeriani et al. 2023, Viswanathan et al. 2025). The paper's contribution is largely empirical packaging of an expected relationship plus a repulsive-loss regularizer closely related to existing contrastive objectives, as the authors themselves concede in B.4.3.

Evidence for the headline causal claim is weak: training experiments use only GPT-2 small trained for 500–1000 steps (test perplexities of 80–300, far from converged models), so claims that 'higher dispersion directly improves perplexity' and that dispersion is a 'functional driver of model performance' are not well supported at realistic training scales.

The kNN-LM layer-selection application (§3.3) is under-evaluated: only dispersion of the final block's attention vs. FFN output is measured for four GPT-2 variants; no actual kNN-LM perplexity results (the very quantity the method claims to predict) are presented in the main text, and the layer search space is limited to two sub-layers of one block rather than 'bypassing exhaustive layer-by-layer searches.'

There is a conspicuous anomaly in Figure 4: 'last-token perplexity' values lie between 1.000 and 1.100, which is implausible for natural text under a trained LM and suggests an error in the experimental setup or metric definition; this is never explained and undermines confidence in that analysis.

Some reported correlations contradict the 'consistently predicts' framing (e.g., r = -0.25, p = 0.017 for Llama-3.1-8B on PubMed), and Figure 2, presented as the motivating 'illustrative empirical trend,' is a synthetic-looking illustration rather than real data placed prominently in the introduction.

The model-selection 'dispersion gap' is validated on very few checkpoints (9 Qwen variants; 4 Llama/CodeLlama pairs), and near-perfect ranking claims ('without a single mis-ordering') rest on tiny samples that could easily reflect the known effect of math/code fine-tuning and distillation on token-embedding norms rather than a general property; no comparison against stronger cheap baselines (e.g., loss on a small sample of domain text, embedding-norm statistics) is provided.

Writing and presentation issues remain: an empty footnote for the code URL ('Code is available at'), a broken LaTeX artifact ('StateMENT ON LLM USAGE'), typos ('di scriminative'), and correlation-vs-causation language that is sometimes stronger than the evidence warrants (despite the honest Limitations section).
